name: Cloud Engineering
tagline: Design, build and run applications on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud — securely and cost-effectively.

overview.summary: Cloud engineers design and operate the infrastructure that modern apps run on: virtual machines, containers, serverless functions, databases, networks and storage on platforms like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). They automate infrastructure with code, keep systems secure and available, and control costs. As AI workloads move to the cloud, cloud engineers also manage GPU capacity, data platforms and AI services.
whyTrending: Robert Half's 2026 technology hiring analysis lists cloud engineering among the five pillars where tech hiring demand is concentrated.
AI adoption drives record cloud spending: companies need engineers to provision GPUs, data pipelines and managed AI services securely.
BLS counts cloud architects within computer network architects — a 2025 median of $134,050 with 8% projected growth (2025–35), much faster than average.
Many Bangladeshi companies and government services are migrating from on-premise servers to cloud or hybrid setups, and offshore firms manage cloud for foreign clients.

stack.note: AWS appears in the most listings worldwide, with Azure strong in enterprise and government. Terraform is the most commonly requested infrastructure-as-code tool.

roadmap.title: Automation and containers
goals: Write Terraform to create a VPC, VM and database

roadmap.title: Architecture and certification

Deploy a three-tier app with autoscaling and a load balancer

interview.question: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?
interview.answer: IaaS gives raw infrastructure (VMs, networks); PaaS gives a managed platform to deploy code (App Service, Cloud Run); SaaS is finished software (Gmail, Salesforce). Each step up means less to manage but less control.

interview.question: What is a VPC and a subnet?
interview.answer: A VPC is your private, isolated network in the cloud. Subnets divide it into IP ranges; public subnets route to the internet, private subnets do not.

interview.question: What is infrastructure as code and why use it?
interview.answer: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files (e.g. Terraform). It makes environments repeatable, reviewable, testable and easy to recreate.

interview.question: How do you make an application highly available?
interview.answer: Run multiple instances across availability zones behind a load balancer, use managed databases with replicas, health checks, autoscaling and automated failover.

interview.question: Vertical vs horizontal scaling?
interview.answer: Vertical adds more CPU/RAM to one machine; horizontal adds more machines. Horizontal scaling is preferred for resilience and elasticity.

interview.question: How do you secure an S3 bucket / storage account?
interview.answer: Block public access, use least-privilege IAM policies, enable encryption and versioning, turn on access logging and use private endpoints where possible.

interview.question: What is a security group vs a network ACL?
interview.answer: Security groups are stateful firewalls attached to resources; network ACLs are stateless rules applied at the subnet level.

interview.question: How would you reduce a cloud bill?
interview.answer: Rightsize instances, shut down idle resources, use autoscaling, reserved or savings plans for steady workloads, spot instances for flexible jobs, and storage lifecycle policies.

interview.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
interview.answer: RTO is how quickly you must restore service after a failure; RPO is how much data loss (in time) is acceptable. They drive backup and DR design.

interview.question: When would you choose serverless over containers?
interview.answer: Serverless suits spiky, event-driven workloads with little ops overhead; containers suit long-running services, custom runtimes or steady high traffic where cost and control matter.
